claims.claim: 66 isolated subnetworks without significant connections to any other TF were observed.
claims.source: In addition, we observed 66 isolated subnetworks without significant connections to any other TF, which illustrated the generally diverse DNA-binding specificity of most TFs in P. aeruginosa (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The results section describes isolated TF subnetworks with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: The network analysis categorized 104 clusters of different DNA sequence preferences for 182 TFs in P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: In summary, the network analysis categorized 104 clusters of different DNA sequence preferences for 182 TFs in P. aeruginosa (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The results section summarizes the clustering of TFs by DNA-binding specificity.

claims.claim: HT-SELEX-generated motifs were longer than the in vivo motifs generated from ChIP data.
claims.source: In general, HT-SELEX-generated motifs were also longer than the in vivo motifs generated from ChIP data, most likely because these in vivo motifs, compared with HT-SELEX-generated motifs, were derived from a much smaller number of binding sites owing to the small genome size.
claims.evidence: The results section compares HT-SELEX motifs to ChIP-derived motifs and provides an explanation.

claims.claim: The motifs ranged from 9 to 28 bp in P. aeruginosa, with the most prevalent length being 16 bp.
claims.source: Analysis of the PWM model length revealed that the motifs ranged from 9 to 28 bp in P. aeruginosa, with the most prevalent length being 16 bp (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The results section provides the range and mode of motif lengths with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: The vast majority (179/199) of the PWM models displayed homodimeric-type binding.
claims.source: Indeed, the vast majority (179/199) of the PWM models displayed homodimeric-type binding (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2), whereas only approx. 10% (20/199) of the PWM models exhibited monomeric binding specificity.
claims.evidence: The results section quantifies the proportion of homodimeric vs. monomeric binding modes.

claims.claim: Only approximately 10% (20/199) of the PWM models exhibited monomeric binding specificity.
claims.source: Indeed, the vast majority (179/199) of the PWM models displayed homodimeric-type binding (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2), whereas only approx. 10% (20/199) of the PWM models exhibited monomeric binding specificity.
claims.evidence: The results section quantifies the proportion of monomeric binding modes.

claims.claim: Most TFs exhibited two identical protein molecules bound in opposite orientations on different DNA strands forming a head-to-head homodimer.
claims.source: Most TFs exhibited two identical protein molecules bound in opposite orientations on different DNA strands forming a head-to-head homodimer, whereas only 16 TFs showed a consecutive binding orientation in the same direction (head-to-tail) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the predominant orientation of homodimeric binding.

claims.claim: Only 16 TFs showed a consecutive binding orientation in the same direction (head-to-tail).
claims.source: Most TFs exhibited two identical protein molecules bound in opposite orientations on different DNA strands forming a head-to-head homodimer, whereas only 16 TFs showed a consecutive binding orientation in the same direction (head-to-tail) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The results section quantifies the number of TFs with head-to-tail binding orientation.

claims.claim: Most of the head-to-tail homodimeric TFs were found to belong to the OmpR family.
claims.source: Interestingly, most of the head-to-tail homodimeric TFs were found to belong to the OmpR family, which is also the main family for the RRs in the TCS (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1B and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The results section identifies a family-specific binding orientation pattern.

claims.claim: The head-to-head orientation is generally preferred by TFs across species, including humans.
claims.source: The head-to-head orientation is generally preferred by TFs across species, including humans (Jolma et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference for the cross-species preference of binding orientation.

claims.claim: 33,709 direct TF–DNA interactions were deduced by scanning the P. aeruginosa PAO1 genome with all PWM models.
claims.source: We used all of the PWM models to scan the P. aeruginosa PAO1 genome and deduced 33,709 direct TF–DNA interactions, which enabled the construction of transcriptional regulatory networks for nine virulence-associated pathways, providing a valuable resource for deciphering the pathogenicity of P. aeruginosa.
claims.evidence: The discussion section summarizes the genome-wide prediction of TF-DNA interactions.

claims.claim: 33,709 significant putative TFBSs were identified (p<1.0e-5).
claims.source: To predict direct interactions between TFs and DNA sequences, we first used the FIMO software (Grant et al., 2011) to scan genome-wide TFBSs for all of the 182 TFs with available PWM models in the P. aeruginosa PAO1 reference genome and identified 33,709 significant putative TFBSs (p<1.0e-5).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of predicted binding sites with a statistical threshold.

claims.claim: More than 36% (65/182) of TFs were predicted to bind to over 100 sites in the 6.3 Mb genome.
claims.source: For individual TFs, the number of TFBSs differed substantially, with more than 36% (65/182) of TFs predicted to bind to over 100 sites in the 6.3 Mb genome (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The results section quantifies the proportion of TFs with high numbers of binding sites.

claims.claim: The putative TFBSs were highly enriched in the intergenic regions than in the gene body regions (negative binomial test, p<2.2e-16).
claims.source: The putative TFBSs were highly enriched in the intergenic regions than in the gene body regions (negative binomial test, p<2.2e-16), with 57% of them densely located within only a 10% fraction of the genome (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The results section reports a statistical test showing enrichment of TFBSs in intergenic regions.

claims.claim: 57% of putative TFBSs were densely located within only a 10% fraction of the genome.
claims.source: The putative TFBSs were highly enriched in the intergenic regions than in the gene body regions (negative binomial test, p<2.2e-16), with 57% of them densely located within only a 10% fraction of the genome (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The results section quantifies the concentration of TFBSs in a small genomic fraction.

claims.claim: EMSA successfully validated 62 pairs of HT-SELEX motif-predicted TF–DNA interactions.
claims.source: In total, EMSA successfully validated 62 pairs of HT-SELEX motif-predicted TF–DNA interactions, including the binding modes (monomeric vs homodimeric binding) of the TFs in each interaction and various monomer spacings and orientations, thus demonstrating the high quality of the data set (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–11).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of experimentally validated TF-DNA interactions.

claims.claim: 37 TFs were predicted to regulate motility-related genes.
claims.source: In sum, 37 TFs were predicted to regulate motility-related genes, in which 10 TFs were predicted to be highly involved regulators including RopN, PA0528, PA1145, PA1399, PA1490, EraR, PA3458, PA3594, PA4508, and PA4659 (Figure 2—figure supplement 12).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of TFs associated with motility.

claims.claim: The target genes of 38% (69/182) of the TFs were enriched for at least one GO term (p<0.05).
claims.source: The target genes of 38% (69/182) of the TFs were enriched for at least one GO term (p<0.05), and 21 functional categories were associated with the regulons of these TFs.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the proportion of TFs with GO term enrichment.

claims.claim: 21 functional categories were associated with the regulons of TFs with GO term enrichment.
claims.source: The target genes of 38% (69/182) of the TFs were enriched for at least one GO term (p<0.05), and 21 functional categories were associated with the regulons of these TFs.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of functional categories identified.

claims.claim: More than 80% of target genes for 20 randomly selected TFs enriched for 'transcription regulator activity' coded for TFs (234/291).
claims.source: We then analyzed and explored the target genes for 20 TFs randomly selected from the 69 genes enriched for 'transcription regulator activity' and found that more than 80% of them coded for TFs (234/291), implying an inter-connective transcriptional regulatory network integrated with mutual regulation between TFs.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the proportion of TF targets that are themselves TFs.

claims.claim: PA0225 (ErfA) is a novel regulator of biofilm production.
claims.source: PA0225 (ErfA) is a novel regulator of biofilm production
claims.evidence: The section heading explicitly identifies PA0225 as a novel biofilm regulator.

claims.claim: 57 putative TFs were predicted to regulate genes involved in biofilm production.
claims.source: In our analysis, 57 putative TFs were predicted to regulate genes involved in biofilm production, including nine previously known regulators such as FleQ (Baraquet and Harwood, 2013; Hickman and Harwood, 2008), AlgB (Chand et al., 2012), and AmrZ (Jones et al., 2014; Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of TFs predicted to regulate biofilm genes.

claims.claim: The deletion of PA0225 significantly decreased the transcriptional activity of pelA down to only one-third of that in wild-type cells.
claims.source: The deletion of PA0225 significantly decreased the transcriptional activity of pelA down to only one-third of that in wild-type (WT) cells.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the effect of PA0225 deletion on pelA transcription.

claims.claim: The depleted pelA expression could be completely restored by ectopic overexpression of PA0225 in the mutant cells.
claims.source: The depleted pelA expression could be completely restored by ectopic overexpression of PA0225 in the mutant cells (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the complementation experiment result.

claims.claim: The intensity of the crystal violet staining ring formed by PA0225 mutant cells was significantly lighter than that formed by WT P. aeruginosa cells.
claims.source: We found that the intensity of the crystal violet staining ring formed by the mutant cells was significantly lighter than that formed by WT P. aeruginosa cells.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the biofilm phenotype of the PA0225 mutant.

claims.claim: The cell adherence phenotype in the PA0225 knockout cells could be effectively recovered by overexpressing PA0225 via transformed pAK1900 plasmid.
claims.source: Like the pelA transcription, the cell adherence phenotype in the knockout cells could also be effectively recovered by overexpressing PA0225 via transformed pAK1900 plasmid, supporting the role of PA0225 in regulating biofilm production (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the complementation of the biofilm phenotype.

claims.claim: More than 100 TF-target gene relationships were predicted in the QS system, involving a total of 49 TFs.
claims.source: By using the PWM models of TFs to scan the genome, we predicted more than 100 TF-target gene relationships that occurred in the QS system, which involved a total of 49 TFs.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of TF-target relationships and TFs in the QS pathway.

claims.claim: PA2497 deletion significantly reduced the transcriptional level of qslA.
claims.source: To further explore the regulatory role of uncharacterized TF binding to this promoter, we generated a clean deletion mutant of TF PA2497 that exhibited a significant decrease in the transcription of qslA compared to the WT strain.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the effect of PA2497 deletion on qslA transcription.

claims.claim: The deficiency in qslA transcription caused by PA2497 deletion could be effectively restored by ectopic overexpression of PA2497 in the mutant strain.
claims.source: The deficiency could be effectively restored by ectopic overexpression of PA2497 in the mutant strain (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the complementation of qslA transcription.

claims.claim: PA1413 deletion significantly reduced the transcriptional level of phzH.
claims.source: PA1413 deletion significantly reduced the transcriptional level of phzH, which could also be reinstated by ectopically expressing PA1413 in the knockout cells (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the effect of PA1413 deletion on phzH transcription.

claims.claim: 37 TFs were identified as involved in the regulation of T6SS, 24 of which were previously uncharacterized.
claims.source: We wired the interactions between TFs and T6SS-related genes and identified 37 TFs involved in the regulation of T6SS, 24 of which were previously uncharacterized (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of TFs associated with T6SS.

claims.claim: TFBSs of up to 10 TFs (GacA, PhoB, PA5293, PA0032, PA2028, PA1437, PA0784, PA1315, PA3249, and PA3225) were putatively found in the amrZ promoter region.
claims.source: In addition to identification of their downstream targets, TFBSs of up to 10 TFs (GacA, PhoB, PA5293, PA0032, PA2028, PA1437, PA0784, PA1315, PA3249, and PA3225) were putatively found in the amrZ promoter region, which suggests a transcriptional regulatory cascade and potential inter-connection between different virulence pathways (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number and identity of TFs predicted to bind the amrZ promoter.

claims.claim: The binding of PhoB to the amrZ promoter was supported by ChIP-seq data and confirmed in vitro by EMSA.
claims.source: Next, we verified the binding sites of TFs using multiple sets of data: the binding of PhoB to the amrZ promoter was supported by ChIP-seq data and confirmed in vitro by EMSA (Figure 5B); the binding sites of the TFs PA1315 and PA3249 were confirmed by EMSA using the genomic fragments covering the amrZ promoter (coordinate: 3,790,981–3,791,197) (Figure 5C,D); the binding site of TF PA0535 to the promoter of the H1-T6SS apparatus component-encoding gene vgrG4 was also validated by EMSA (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The results section reports validation of PhoB binding by multiple methods.

claims.claim: The binding sites of the TFs PA1315 and PA3249 to the amrZ promoter were confirmed by EMSA.
claims.source: Next, we verified the binding sites of TFs using multiple sets of data: the binding of PhoB to the amrZ promoter was supported by ChIP-seq data and confirmed in vitro by EMSA (Figure 5B); the binding sites of the TFs PA1315 and PA3249 were confirmed by EMSA using the genomic fragments covering the amrZ promoter (coordinate: 3,790,981–3,791,197) (Figure 5C,D); the binding site of TF PA0535 to the promoter of the H1-T6SS apparatus component-encoding gene vgrG4 was also validated by EMSA (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The results section reports EMSA validation of PA1315 and PA3249 binding.

claims.claim: The binding site of TF PA0535 to the promoter of vgrG4 was validated by EMSA.
claims.source: Next, we verified the binding sites of TFs using multiple sets of data: the binding of PhoB to the amrZ promoter was supported by ChIP-seq data and confirmed in vitro by EMSA (Figure 5B); the binding sites of the TFs PA1315 and PA3249 were confirmed by EMSA using the genomic fragments covering the amrZ promoter (coordinate: 3,790,981–3,791,197) (Figure 5C,D); the binding site of TF PA0535 to the promoter of the H1-T6SS apparatus component-encoding gene vgrG4 was also validated by EMSA (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The results section reports EMSA validation of PA0535 binding.

claims.claim: PhoB was predicted to influence antibiotic resistance by binding to the promoters of pstB, oprD, PA3516, and czcABC.
claims.source: The TF PhoB was predicted to influence antibiotic resistance by binding to the promoters of pstB, oprD, PA3516, and czcABC, which was confirmed by both ChIP-seq (Bielecki et al., 2015) and EMSA (Figure 2—figure supplement 7B–E).
claims.evidence: The results section reports predicted and validated PhoB binding sites in antibiotic resistance genes.

claims.claim: 16 novel TFs could putatively bind to at least three siderophore-associated genes.
claims.source: The siderophore network revealed that 16 novel TFs could putatively bind to at least three siderophore-associated genes, with some loci co-bound by more than one TFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of novel TFs associated with siderophore genes.

claims.claim: 26, 17, and 11 TFs were predicted to be associated with the regulation of T3SS, ROS, and the SR and persistence pathways, respectively.
claims.source: Furthermore, 26, 17, and 11 TFs were predicted to be associated with the regulation of T3SS, ROS, and the SR and persistence pathways, respectively.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of TFs associated with three additional pathways.

claims.claim: Among the TFs associated with T3SS, ROS, and SR/persistence pathways, 17, 11, and 8 factors, respectively, had not been functionally characterized before.
claims.source: Among them, 17, 11, and 8 factors, respectively, had not been functionally characterized before (Figure 2—figure supplement 10, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of uncharacterized TFs in three pathways.

claims.claim: PhoB and its target TF gene amrZ were likely implicated in virtually all virulence-associated pathways.
claims.source: For example, PhoB and its target TF gene amrZ were likely implicated in virtually all virulence-associated pathways, including biofilm production, QS pathway, T6SS, T3SS, antibiotic resistance, and motility.
claims.evidence: The results section identifies PhoB and amrZ as multi-pathway regulators.

claims.claim: PA0048 putative target genes were implicated in biofilm production (mvfR), the QS pathway (rhlB), T6SS (tss), antibiotic resistance (pstB), and the persistence pathway (dnaJ).
claims.source: Similar findings were observed for other factors, such as PA0048, whose putative target genes were implicated in biofilm production (mvfR), the QS pathway (rhlB), T6SS (tss), antibiotic resistance (pstB), and the persistence pathway (dnaJ).
claims.evidence: The results section identifies PA0048 as a multi-pathway regulator.

claims.claim: This study successfully generated 199 unique PWM models to describe the DNA-binding specificities of 182 distinct TFs in P. aeruginosa, which covered nearly 50% of all TFs in its genome.
claims.source: In this study, we successfully generated 199 unique PWM models to describe the DNA-binding specificities of 182 distinct TFs in P. aeruginosa, which covered nearly 50% of all TFs (including putative TFs) in its genome.
claims.evidence: The discussion section summarizes the main achievement of the study.

claims.claim: The DNA-binding specificity of a TF determines where it binds to the genome and which genes it regulates.
claims.source: The DNA-binding specificity of a TF determines where it binds to the genome and which genes it regulates, and this property has notable effects on the physiological activity of the organism.
claims.evidence: The results section states a fundamental principle of TF function.

claims.claim: TF dimer formation events depend on the DNA molecules they interact with, and display strong enrichment for specific monomer orientation and spacing.
claims.source: Early studies have shown that some TF dimer formation events depend on the DNA molecules they interact with, and display strong enrichment for specific monomer orientation and spacing, unlike independent binding events by two monomers that may allow any spacing or orientation between them (Jolma et al., 2013; Jolma et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references for the DNA-dependent nature of TF dimerization.

claims.claim: PhoB binds to DNA as a homodimer in a head-to-tail consecutive orientation, with a 'GTCA(C/T)' monomer sequence preference spaced by a stretch of 6 bp AT-rich nucleotides.
claims.source: For example, the TF PhoB binds to DNA as a homodimer in a head-to-tail consecutive orientation, with a 'GTCA(C/T)' monomer sequence preference spaced by a stretch of 6 bp AT-rich nucleotides (Figure 1C), supported by independent sets of ChIP-seq experiments (Huang et al., 2019; Bielecki et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the binding mode of PhoB with citation support.

claims.claim: Many TFs have been confirmed to act as dimers when binding to DNA, such as LasR, RsaL, PsrA, FleQ, and QscR.
claims.source: Consistently, many TFs have been confirmed to act as dimers when binding to DNA, such as LasR (Bottomley et al., 2007; Fan et al., 2013), RsaL (Kang et al., 2017), PsrA (Kang et al., 2009; Kojic et al., 2002), FleQ (Su et al., 2015), and QscR (Wysoczynski-Horita et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The results section cites multiple references confirming dimeric binding of specific TFs.

claims.claim: The vast majority of TF binding within the gene body region has little or no effect on the transcriptional level in prokaryotes.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that the vast majority of TF binding within the gene body region has little or no effect on the transcriptional level in prokaryotes (Shimada et al., 2008); therefore, we primarily focused on TFBSs in the intergenic regions in the subsequent analyses.
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference for the functional significance of TF binding location.

claims.claim: Nine pathways function in P. aeruginosa to exert its virulence: biofilm production, quorum sensing, Type VI and Type III secretion systems, motility, antibiotic resistance, siderophores, stringent response and persistence, and oxidative stress resistance.
claims.source: To colonize and overwhelm host tissues, nine pathways function in P. aeruginosa to exert its virulence, including biofilm production (Whiteley et al., 2001), quorum sensing (QS) (Lee and Zhang, 2015), Type VI (Ho et al., 2014) and Type III secretion systems (T6SS and T3SS, respectively) (Hauser, 2009; Hovey and Frank, 1995; Brutinel et al., 2008), motility (Coleman et al., 2020), antibiotic resistance (Chen et al., 2010), siderophores (Little et al., 2018), stringent response (SR) and persistence (Moradali et al., 2017; Goodman et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016), and oxidative stress resistance (Lan et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The results section lists the nine virulence pathways with citations.

claims.claim: A TF was annotated as associated with a virulence-associated pathway when its binding sites were significantly enriched within promoters of genes in that pathway (FDR < 0.05).
claims.source: We carried out enrichment analysis of TF-binding sites located in promoter of genes involved in various functional pathways by the hypergeometric test: a TF was annotated association with a virulence-associated pathway when its binding sites were significantly enriched within promoters of genes in that pathway (FDR < 0.05).
claims.evidence: The results section describes the statistical method for associating TFs with pathways.

claims.claim: Biofilm is a complex community of diverse or single types of bacterial colonies embedded in an extracellular polymeric matrix that contains water, exopolysaccharides, extracellular DNA, proteins, and type IV pili.
claims.source: Biofilm is a complex community of diverse or single types of bacterial colonies embedded in an extracellular polymeric matrix that contains water, exopolysaccharides, extracellular DNA, proteins, and type IV pili (Tseng et al., 2018; Burrows, 2012; Laventie et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references defining biofilm composition.

claims.claim: P. aeruginosa produces biofilms to protect itself from host defense and antimicrobial agents, which helps enhance its pathogenicity.
claims.source: P. aeruginosa produces biofilms to protect itself from host defense and antimicrobial agents, which helps enhance its pathogenicity (Mulcahy et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference for the protective function of biofilms.

claims.claim: Approximately 20 TFs have been reported to influence biofilm production.
claims.source: To date, approximately 20 TFs have been reported to influence biofilm production (Kang et al., 2017; Badal et al., 2020; Baraquet and Harwood, 2013; Hickman and Harwood, 2008; Baraquet et al., 2012; Dieppois et al., 2012; Parkins et al., 2001; Petrova and Sauer, 2009; Vallet et al., 2004; Monds et al., 2001; Ernst et al., 1999; Macfarlane et al., 1999; Ramsey and Whiteley, 2004; McPhee et al., 2006; Liang et al., 2008; Nicastro et al., 2009; Mikkelsen et al., 2009; Mukherjee et al., 2017; Finelli et al., 2003; Damron et al., 2009; Kong et al., 2015; Deretic and Konyecsni, 1990; Balasubramanian et al., 2012; Hammond et al., 2015; Petrova and Sauer, 2010; Petrova et al., 2011; Guragain et al., 2016; Sarkisova et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2019; Yeung et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The results section cites multiple references for known biofilm regulators.

claims.claim: Multiple TFs, including AmrZ, FleQ, PA5293, and PA4547, were predicted to bind to the same psl operon.
claims.source: For instance, multiple TFs, including AmrZ, FleQ, and two uncharacterized TFs, PA5293 and PA4547, were predicted to bind to the same psl operon (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The results section reports co-binding of multiple TFs to the psl operon.

claims.claim: AmrZ was previously reported to bind to the psl operon and repressed its transcription, consequently decreasing biofilm production.
claims.source: Consistently, AmrZ was previously reported to bind to the psl operon and repressed its transcription, consequently decreasing biofilm production (Jones et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference for AmrZ function in biofilm regulation.

claims.claim: A very strong AmrZ ChIP-seq peak was identified for the psl promoter containing the PWM-predicted binding site (Coordinates: 2,453,511–2,453,531).
claims.source: A very strong AmrZ ChIP-seq peak was identified for the psl promoter containing our PWM-predicted binding site (Coordinates: 2,453,511–2,453,531) (Jones et al., 2014; Figure 3B), supporting the precise prediction of the binding site by our PWM motif.
claims.evidence: The results section cites ChIP-seq data validating the predicted AmrZ binding site.

claims.claim: FleQ was previously observed to bind to the psl operon and consequently decrease biofilm production.
claims.source: In addition, FleQ was previously observed to bind to the psl operon and consequently decrease biofilm production (Hickman and Harwood, 2008; Jones et al., 2013; Baraquet and Harwood, 2016).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references for FleQ function in biofilm regulation.

claims.claim: FleQ and three uncharacterized factors, PA0225 (ErfA), PA0191, and PA1241, putatively bound the promoter of the pelABCDEFG operon.
claims.source: In addition to the psl operon, we found that FleQ and three uncharacterized factors, PA0225 (ErfA) (Trouillon et al., 2020), PA0191, and PA1241, putatively bound the promoter of another biofilm-associated operon pelABCDEFG (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The results section reports predicted binding of multiple TFs to the pel operon.

claims.claim: The binding of FleQ to the promoter of pel clusters had been verified by a footprint assay in a previous study.
claims.source: The binding of FleQ to the promoter of pel clusters had been verified by a footprint assay in a previous study (Baraquet and Harwood, 2016).
claims.evidence: The results section cites a reference for FleQ binding to the pel promoter.

claims.claim: P. aeruginosa biofilm production is sensitive to the cellular abundance of PelA.
claims.source: It is known that P. aeruginosa biofilm production is sensitive to the cellular abundance of PelA (Friedman and Kolter, 2004; Ryder et al., 2007), and therefore we attempted to investigate whether the deletion of PA0225 could consequently lead to deficiency in biofilm formation, given that PA0225 was a potential regulator of pelA expression.
claims.evidence: The results section cites references for the role of PelA in biofilm production.

claims.claim: Transposon-mediated mutant strains of 57 putative biofilm-associated TFs were obtained, except PA2121, PA2118, and PA2028, due to lack of availability.
claims.source: To comprehensively validate the list of TFs putatively associated with biofilm production, we obtained transposon-mediated mutant strains of 57 putative biofilm-associated TFs (Jacobs et al., 2003) except PA2121, PA2118, and PA2028, due to lack of availability.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of mutant strains obtained for validation.

claims.claim: The depletion of known regulators such as AmrZ, FleQ, or PA0191 significantly affected biofilm formation.
claims.source: Using a crystal violet assay, we confirmed that the depletion of known regulators such as AmrZ, FleQ, or PA0191 significantly affected biofilm formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: The results section reports validation of known biofilm regulators using mutant strains.

claims.claim: Both activating and repressing phenotypes could be observed upon manipulating TF binding in P. aeruginosa.
claims.source: Similar to other prokaryotic TFs, both activating and repressing phenotypes could be observed upon manipulating TF binding in P. aeruginosa (Yang et al., 2019; Poole et al., 1996; Kawalek et al., 2019; Ha et al., 2004; Wu and Jin, 2005; Jin et al., 2011; Daddaoua et al., 2017; Chugani et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references for the dual regulatory roles of TFs.

claims.claim: QS is a bacterial cell–cell communication system that fine-tunes the expression of hundreds of genes to produce, release, and recognize signaling molecules to monitor cell numbers and synchronize group behaviors.
claims.source: QS is a bacterial cell–cell communication system that fine-tunes the expression of hundreds of genes to produce, release, and recognize signaling molecules to monitor cell numbers and synchronize group behaviors (Lee and Zhang, 2015; Williams and Cámara, 2009; Høyland-Kroghsbo et al., 2017), while mediating cross-talks with a variety of virulence pathways involved in the aforementioned biofilm production and other important pathways such as T6SS, T3SS, motility, and antibiotic resistance (Lee and Zhang, 2015; Williams and Cámara, 2009).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references defining QS and its functions.

claims.claim: More than 100 TF-target gene relationships were predicted in the QS system.
claims.source: By using the PWM models of TFs to scan the genome, we predicted more than 100 TF-target gene relationships that occurred in the QS system, which involved a total of 49 TFs.
claims.evidence: The results section reports the number of predicted TF-target relationships in QS.

claims.claim: Four TFs had been previously annotated with regulatory roles in QS: Anr, PsrA, PhoB, and RsaL.
claims.source: In the putative QS network, four TFs had been previously annotated with regulatory roles in QS: Anr (Hammond et al., 2015), PsrA (Wells et al., 2017), PhoB (Blus-Kadosh et al., 2013), and RsaL (Kang et al., 2017; Figure 4A, Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: The results section cites references for known QS regulators.

claims.claim: PhoB putatively conferred an auto-regulatory activity, with a predicted binding site on its own promoter.
claims.source: Our analysis showed that PhoB putatively conferred an auto-regulatory activity, with a predicted binding site on its own promoter (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The results section reports predicted auto-regulation of PhoB.

claims.claim: A very strong ChIP-seq peak was identified for PhoB in the intergenic region upstream of its own transcription starting site, with its summit close to the PWM-predicted binding site (coordinate: 6,299,632–6,299,648).
claims.source: When we inspected the in vivo PhoB binding in the intergenic region upstream of its own transcription starting site, a very strong ChIP-seq peak was identified with its summit close to that of our PWM-predicted binding site (coordinate: 6,299,632–6,299,648) (Bielecki et al., 2015; Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The results section cites ChIP-seq data validating PhoB auto-regulation.

results.result: HT-SELEX was applied to 371 putative TFs in P. aeruginosa PAO1, generating 199 PWM models describing the DNA-binding specificities of 182 TFs with high reproducibility across technical replicates.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C17-C23 collectively describe the HT-SELEX experimental design, execution, and output. The methodology is clearly described, the success rate (49%) is quantified, and reproducibility is demonstrated through 12 independent replicates showing virtually identical binding specificities. The data are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Network analysis of PWM similarity revealed 104 clusters of DNA sequence preferences, with 133 PWM models from 116 TFs forming 38 interconnected subnetworks and 66 isolated subnetworks.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 describe the network analysis results using SSTAT similarity scoring. The clustering analysis is methodologically sound and the numbers are internally consistent (38 interconnected + 66 isolated = 104 total clusters). The analysis appropriately characterizes the diversity of TF binding specificities.

results.result: Most TFs (179/199, 90%) bind DNA as homodimers, predominantly in head-to-head orientation, with motif lengths ranging from 9-28 bp (mode 16 bp). Head-to-tail binding is enriched in the OmpR family.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C34 characterize the binding modes and motif properties. The quantitative data are clearly presented with appropriate proportions and the head-to-tail enrichment in OmpR family is supported by citation C34. The comparison to ChIP-derived motifs (C27) provides reasonable explanation for observed differences.

results.result: Genome-wide scanning identified 33,709 significant TFBSs (p<1.0e-5) that were highly enriched (>11-fold, p<2.2e-16) in intergenic regions, with 57% located in only 10% of the genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C39 describe the genome-wide prediction of TF binding sites with appropriate statistical thresholds and enrichment analysis. The negative binomial test for intergenic enrichment is appropriate, and the concentration of binding sites is well-quantified. The p-value threshold choice is justified in the methods.

results.result: EMSA validated 62 pairs of HT-SELEX motif-predicted TF-DNA interactions, including binding modes and various monomer spacings and orientations.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 reports experimental validation of predicted binding sites. The EMSA validation is shown in multiple supplementary figures and provides orthogonal confirmation of the HT-SELEX predictions. The validation includes diverse binding modes, strengthening confidence in the predictions.

results.result: 51 TFs were significantly associated with nine virulence-associated pathways (FDR<0.05), including 32 previously uncharacterized TFs, with some TFs involved in multiple pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7, C72-C73 describe the pathway enrichment analysis using hypergeometric testing with appropriate multiple testing correction (FDR<0.05). The identification of 32 novel TFs represents a major advance. The statistical approach is sound and the multi-pathway involvement is well-documented.

results.result: PA0225 (ErfA) is a novel regulator of biofilm production that binds the pelABCDEFG promoter, with deletion reducing pelA transcription to one-third of wild-type levels and significantly decreasing biofilm formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50, C81-C83 provide comprehensive evidence for PA0225 as a biofilm regulator through EMSA validation (C48), RT-qPCR showing transcriptional effects (C47), complementation experiments (C48, C50), and crystal violet biofilm assays (C49-C50). The experimental design includes appropriate controls and complementation, supporting the regulatory role.

results.result: 49 TFs were predicted to regulate quorum sensing genes with >100 TF-target relationships, including novel regulators PA2497 (regulating qslA) validated by deletion and complementation experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C87-C96 describe the QS regulatory network with experimental validation. The prediction of co-binding by multiple TFs (C92, C95-C96) is validated by EMSA for at least 6 TFs. The functional validation of PA2497 through deletion and complementation (C52-C53) provides strong evidence for the predicted regulatory relationships.

results.result: PA1413 regulates phzH (phenazine synthesis), with deletion significantly reducing phzH transcription and complementation restoring expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C54 and C97 describe the regulatory relationship between PA1413 and phzH with experimental validation through deletion and complementation. The experimental design is appropriate and the phenazine synthesis pathway is well-established (C97 citation), providing context for the finding.

results.result: 37 TFs regulate T6SS genes (24 previously uncharacterized), with up to 10 TFs binding the amrZ promoter. Binding of PhoB, PA1315, PA3249, and PA0535 to T6SS promoters was validated by EMSA and/or ChIP-seq.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59, C98-C104 describe the T6SS regulatory network with multiple lines of validation. The convergence of HT-SELEX predictions, ChIP-seq data (C57), and EMSA validation (C57-C59) for multiple TFs provides strong support. The identification of 10 TFs binding amrZ (C56) suggests complex regulatory cascades.

results.result: 37 TFs regulate motility genes, including 10 highly involved regulators. The network shares regulators with biofilm production (FleQ, AlgB, AmrZ) but also includes distinct TFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C105-C108 describe the motility regulatory network. The prediction of FleQ binding to flhA is supported by independent literature (C107), and the identification of shared and distinct regulators with biofilm production is biologically coherent. The quantification of 10 highly involved regulators is clearly stated.

results.result: TFs were predicted to regulate antibiotic resistance (18 TFs, 11 novel), siderophores (16 novel TFs), T3SS (26 TFs, 17 novel), ROS (17 TFs, 11 novel), and SR/persistence (11 TFs, 8 novel). PhoB binding to antibiotic resistance gene promoters was validated by ChIP-seq and EMSA.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63, C109-C110 describe regulatory networks for five additional virulence pathways. The validation of PhoB binding by both ChIP-seq and EMSA (C60) provides strong support for at least some predictions. The identification of numerous novel TFs across pathways represents a significant resource, though most lack experimental validation.

results.result: Some TFs, including PhoB/amrZ and PA0048, are implicated in multiple virulence pathways, suggesting inter-pathway connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 identify multi-pathway regulators. The evidence for PhoB and amrZ involvement across pathways is supported by multiple validated binding sites throughout the manuscript. PA0048 targets in multiple pathways are predicted but less extensively validated. The concept of inter-pathway connectivity is well-supported.

results.result: GO enrichment analysis revealed functional associations for 69 TFs (38%) across 21 categories. Over 80% of targets for TFs enriched in 'transcription regulator activity' were themselves TFs, suggesting interconnected regulatory networks. Novel functions were suggested for 46 uncharacterized TFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44, C111-C116 describe GO enrichment analysis results. The finding that 80% of TF targets are themselves TFs (C44, C112) is based on analysis of 20 randomly selected TFs and supports the concept of hierarchical regulatory networks. The functional predictions for uncharacterized TFs (C113-C116) are hypothesis-generating but appropriately presented as potential associations.

results.result: Transposon mutant validation of 54 biofilm-associated TFs confirmed that depletion of known regulators (AmrZ, FleQ, PA0191) significantly affected biofilm formation, though most mutants showed no overt phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 describe transposon mutant validation with mixed results. While known regulators showed expected phenotypes (C85), most mutants did not (C86). The authors attribute this to polar effects of transposon insertion, which is plausible but limits the validation. The lack of phenotypes for many predicted regulators raises questions about false positive predictions or experimental limitations.

results.result: The study generated 199 PWM models covering nearly 50% of P. aeruginosa TFs. TF binding specificity determines genomic binding locations and gene regulation, with dimer formation depending on DNA sequence and showing specific orientation/spacing preferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 summarize the study's scope and provide mechanistic context. The 50% coverage (C66) is a major achievement. The mechanistic principles (C67-C68) are well-established and appropriately cited. The specific example of PhoB binding mode (C69) is validated by independent ChIP-seq data, and the general principle of dimeric binding (C70) is supported by multiple citations.

results.result: TF-binding specificity is conserved across species, with P. aeruginosa PhoB showing high similarity to C. crescentus PhoB, and orthologous TFs from different strains displaying similar binding specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 describe evolutionary conservation of TF binding specificity. The comparison to C. crescentus PhoB (C117) and the general principle of conservation (C118) are both supported by appropriate citations. This provides additional validation for the HT-SELEX-derived motifs and suggests broader applicability of the findings.

results.result: P. aeruginosa causes significant morbidity and mortality (>2 million infections, ~90,000 deaths annually). Virulence regulation is controlled by TFs, but less than 5% of ~400 predicted TFs have characterized DNA-binding specificities.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C16 provide background context. The clinical significance (C8-C10) is cited to a 1983 reference (Cross et al.), which may be outdated for current infection/mortality statistics. The general principles about TF function (C11-C13) are well-established. The gap in TF characterization (C14-C16) motivates the study, though the exact percentages depend on the cited reference (Huang et al., 2019).

results.result: Biofilm production involves exopolysaccharides including Pel and Psl. Multiple TFs (AmrZ, FleQ, PA5293, PA4547) co-bind the psl operon, with AmrZ and FleQ binding validated by ChIP-seq and previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 describe biofilm biology and regulatory mechanisms. The biofilm composition (C74-C75) and known regulators (C76) are well-cited. The co-binding of multiple TFs to psl (C77) is predicted, with AmrZ binding validated by strong ChIP-seq peak at the predicted site (C79) and FleQ binding supported by previous studies (C80, C82). This demonstrates the quality of predictions.
